name: Scripted sessions that end right and requirements met
purpose: A scripted session answers every turn and ends cleanly, and a person working with the AI while it works can watch, stop, resume, steer, see helpers, approve and read the result on two harnesses.
record: One number: the share of scripted-stdin sessions that come out right (every turn reaches the front door in order, nothing a person typed is lost, a question is answered by the next line, the wanted text is shown, the session ends cleanly), balanced with time by [balance.terminal_session]; weights and budgets fixed in esoi.toml before any arm was scored. Kinds of case, as case sources of one component: turn, command, ask, exit (evaluation/terminal_session/build_cases.py). First stage, model-free: a stub front door answers each line from the case, so the check costs nothing. Later stages (a real offline run of the whole hub, a person's trial) rise in fidelity and keep this number. Added case kind attend (live helper reported by the loop itself, a stop during a slow model call, a tree of solution workers, the structure toggled and opened, ceilings, the soft-limit and stop-decision lines, the end of a run, a follow-up that continues the session, a harness switch, the no-goal prompt and the Representative, beside the earlier scenarios) (evaluation/terminal_session/sessions.py): scripted sessions on the hub's own loop (a scripted completion behind the loop runner) and on a fake that keeps the stream runner's contract, each scored by named checks against requirement ids X1 to X23 of docs/explanation/working-with-the-ai-while-it-works.md; the share of cases right is the number, and per-requirement shares are reported. Added case kinds on 2026-11-10: documented (nine scenarios taken from what the reviewed terminals document and from the consumer's requirement tests, driven with raw stream-json lines and typed events that know no arm: a refused command shows its reason, a helper's file counts as changed, a run is not met while a helper works, the first seconds show a start, a message is queued until read, a helper's question names the helper, the answer's markdown is rendered, a stopped run keeps its work and names the resume command, a run that changed nothing says so) and pty (the real entry point: `ahohs work` on a pseudo-terminal, python pty, with a real fast-tier session on the Claude CLI login, nine scenarios: complete run, Escape then resume, steer, structure open, follow-up, harness switch, a refused command, a long markdown answer, input history; a key is sent when a file appears, a run is over when its worker process is gone, what the person saw is the text the terminal printed; evaluation/terminal_session/pty_stage.py). Run the real stage with `--max-calls`. The real stage runs with --max-calls (esoi run terminal_session --impl <arm> --record --max-calls 40).
disadvantages: Few invented sessions against a stub front door: it shows the loop holds, not that a person finds the screen clear. The pseudo-terminal stage has no terminal emulator, so what stays on a full-screen screen (scrollback, a menu, the mouse) is not judged, only the text the terminal printed and the files; a person's trial is still the later stage. Scripted harnesses prove the contract, not that a real model's run feels right; a person's trial on a real terminal is the later stage.
cascading_conditionals: free [sample=full | real=no | gate=all-pass | when=the arm was recorded on the same cases]

name: Terminal screen as drawn (presentation) after the correctness gate
purpose: A terminal arm is ranked by how its screen is drawn for a person working with the AI, once it does what the requirements say: every update shown once, the current step in view, finished work kept across a stop, a correction shown as sent then taken up, a risky step waiting with its preview, a complete closing report, rows that fit, calm redraw, readable contrast, plain output when not a terminal, whole key hints, a quick first output, and every control reaching the harness with an acknowledgement or a plain notice that it is not available. It ensures the arm that opens bare `ahohs` is chosen on the screen a person sees, not on a script that cannot see it.
record: Layer 1, the number: the weighted share of the named checks passed, over the same scripted sessions on a scripted fake harness (no model), each drawn at 80x24 and 120x40 and read back from the emulated screen: the terminal emulator pyte (LGPL-3.0, an evaluation-only dependency) for an arm that writes to a stream, Textual's run_test for a Textual arm (drawn by the arm's own application and transcript where it has one: a capture hook in presentation_of, added on 2026-11-11 when polished_session was first scored, with no check or weight changed), and an external client in a pseudo-terminal through the same emulator. Checks (evaluation/terminal_presentation/checks.py, each tied to requirements X1 to X33): each update shown once (no duplicate row, nothing in both the live region and the scrollback), current step visible, stop then resume keeps work, correction sent then taken up, risky step waits with its preview, closing report complete, no row wider than the terminal and no sideways scroll, repaints at most 10 a second with at most 4 cursor jumps each, contrast 4.5:1 (3:1 for decoration), plain when not a terminal, key hints present and whole, first output within one second, and the control round trips (stop, resume, steer, approve, refuse reach the harness and show an acknowledgement; a control the surface cannot do is shown as not available). A case scores the weighted share of the checks that applied; weights and their reasons are fixed in esoi.toml [balance.terminal_presentation.check_weights] before any arm was scored; the balanced score is [balance.terminal_presentation]. The protocol ceiling column is reported beside it and is not scored: hub information a surface cannot show at all (the structure tree on request, spend against ceilings, who the AI acts for, a correction shown as taken up, stopping one helper) is a miss there and not a rendering fault. Layer 2, advisory and never the gate: a model judges six fixed frames (start, mid run, waiting, stopped, finished, narrow) as text grids against a frozen checklist of 15 yes or no items drawn from Nielsen's ten heuristics, the Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (CHI 2019) and clig.dev, quoting the frame for every yes, three runs and a majority, arms blinded and shuffled, tier by the role deliverable_judge, read with its miss rate on a calibration set of 12 frames with injected defects (evaluation/terminal_presentation/judged). The harness and the calibration set are built; layer 2 has not been run on any arm. The correctness gate is metric-terminal-session (its scripted sessions on two harnesses): an arm that fails any of its cases is not ranked on presentation.
disadvantages: Layer 1 reads the screen of a scripted session, not a person: it cannot say whether the screen is clear, only whether named, checkable faults are absent, so two arms can tie on it and the person's trial stays the later stage. The checks are the owner's requirements restated, so an arm built to them is not tested against a fault nobody listed. Contrast assumes a dark default terminal background (a cell with no colour of its own is judged against black) and reads SGR faint (SGR 2) as half intensity, which cannot be known: the ECMA-48 definition is only decreased intensity, and published reports differ (some terminals halve the intensity, others show no change at all; https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/terminal-wg/specifications/-/issues/27, https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/vte/-/issues/2462, https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij/pull/1803, https://bugs.kde.org/show_bug.cgi?id=480843; secondhand reports, not read in any terminal's source), so the check judges the worst case and an arm that avoids faint for informative text cannot fail it; the Textual capture reads Textual's compositor, an internal of Textual, so a Textual release can change it; the flicker bound is on the repaints a stream arm writes and does not apply to Textual's differential renderer (not applicable, left out of the share); one scripted harness cannot show how a real model's run feels. The weights are judgement fixed in advance with reasons, not fitted. Layer 2 is advisory because published studies find model-judged usability evaluation unreliable (Guerino et al. 2025, arXiv 2506.16345: it found only a small share of the issues experts found, with false positives; Zhong et al. 2025, arXiv 2507.02306: more issues than experts on app screenshots, but weak on conventions and across screens, and on screenshots of graphical apps, not terminal grids), so it can only order arms layer 1 ties on, after its miss rate is known, and never overrides layer 1.
cascading_conditionals: layer1 [sample=full | real=no | gate=competitive | when=the arm passed every case of metric-terminal-session (esoi run terminal_session --impl the arm) so it is ranked on its screen only once it does what the requirements say; free, no model; run on the arm and its rivals on the same cases; arms tied here are ordered by the protocol ceiling column, then by layer 2 only after its calibration miss rate is recorded; a person's trial on a real terminal with a real harness is the later stage and is not a stage here (a free row would be counted as passing it); no arm is run live just to fill a row]
command: esoi run terminal_presentation --impl live_session; esoi run terminal_presentation --impl textual_session; esoi run terminal_session --impl live_session
